title: Progress reporting: purpose & benefits
blurb: Outline why projects report progress, the benefits it brings, and how time-driven, event-driven and RAG reporting work.
question: A sponsor complains that she only hears about problems on her ferry terminal project when they are already serious. What is the purpose of progress reporting, and what benefits should good reporting give her?

teach.h: Telling decision-makers where the project really is
teach.body: The purpose of progress reporting is to communicate the project's status, actual performance compared with the baseline, to the sponsor and other stakeholders, so that timely decisions and corrective actions can be taken. Plainly: it tells the people who can act how the project is doing against what was agreed, early enough for them to do something about it.

teach.h: Where reporting fits in monitoring and control
teach.caption: Reporting turns measurements into information that decision-makers can act on.

head: Benefit
What it gives the project
rows: Variances and problems spotted while still fixable
The sponsor decides on facts, not guesswork
A view of when and at what cost it will finish
Stakeholders trust an honest, regular picture
A record of performance and decisions over time
Highlights what needs attention or escalation

teach.h: What a typical progress report contains
items: Status against the baseline: schedule, cost, scope and quality.
Achievements this period and work planned for the next.
Forecast to completion: likely end date and final cost.
Key risks and issues, and what is being done about them.
Decisions or support needed from the sponsor or board.

rows.label: Weakness
values: No regular picture if used alone

teach.caption: Most projects use both: a regular cycle of reports, plus event-driven reports when milestones are reached or tolerances are threatened.

bands.label: Green: on track against the baseline
Amber: problems, but recoverable within tolerance
Red: off track; tolerance breached or about to be

teach.caption: Typical meanings. Each organisation defines its own RAG thresholds, so reports should say what each colour means.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Harbour Point ferry terminal
head: Area
RAG
Comment
rows: Two weeks behind: late steel; recovery plan in place
Winter storms could stop piling work
teach.caption: This is the monthly (time-driven) report. When the steel supplier later fails, the PM sends an event-driven exception report: schedule Red, decision needed.

teach.text: Progress reporting is about tracking and communicating status against the baseline so decisions can be made. It does not shorten the critical path, create float, or secure acceptance of deliverables. And a report that stays Green while problems grow defeats its purpose.

teach.h: Good reports are honest and tailored
teach.body: A report is only useful if it is accurate, timely and acted on. Tailor the level of detail to the audience: the board needs a summary and the decisions required, while the team needs task-level detail. Report bad news early and plainly, with a recovery plan. Hiding problems behind optimistic colours removes the early warning the sponsor relies on.

items: Purpose: communicate status (actual vs baseline) so timely decisions and corrective action can be taken.
Benefits: early warning, informed decisions, forecasting, transparency, confidence, audit trail, visibility of risks and issues.
Time-driven reports follow a regular cycle; event-driven reports follow milestones, gates or exceptions.
RAG gives an at-a-glance status: Green on track, Amber at risk, Red off track.

summary: You can now outline the purpose of progress reporting, communicating actual performance against the baseline so timely decisions can be made, and list its benefits. You can tell time-driven from event-driven reports and interpret RAG status.

A.q: What is the main purpose of project progress reporting?
options: To communicate status against the baseline for decisions
To lengthen the float available on non-critical tasks
To secure user acceptance of the finished outputs
To record lessons learned once the project has closed
A.why: Progress reporting communicates actual performance against the baseline so that the sponsor and stakeholders can make timely decisions.

whyNot.1: Reporting does not change float; float comes from the schedule's logic.
whyNot.2: Acceptance of outputs is part of quality control and handover, not the purpose of reporting.
whyNot.3: Lessons learned are captured in a post-project review, not by progress reporting.

A.q: Which of the following is an example of a time-driven report?
options: A report issued when a milestone is reached
A monthly highlight report to the board
An exception report when tolerance is at risk
A report triggered by a decision gate review
A.why: A time-driven report is produced on a regular calendar cycle, such as monthly.

whyNot.0: A report triggered by reaching a milestone is event-driven.
whyNot.2: An exception report is triggered by an event, a threatened tolerance.
whyNot.3: A report triggered by a gate is event-driven.

A.q: In RAG reporting, what does an Amber status typically signal?
options: Work is complete and has been accepted
The project is on track with no concerns
Problems exist but should be recoverable
Tolerance is breached; a decision is needed
A.why: Amber typically means there are problems or risks, but they are expected to be recoverable within tolerance.

whyNot.0: RAG shows status against plan; completion and acceptance are not what Amber means.
whyNot.1: On track with no concerns is Green.
whyNot.3: A breached tolerance needing a sponsor decision is Red.

B.q: Which of the following is a benefit of regular progress reporting?
options: It removes the need for a risk register
It guarantees the project finishes on time
It replaces the need for decision gates
It gives early warning of variances
B.why: Regular reporting surfaces variances early, while there is still time to correct them.

whyNot.0: Reports draw on the risk register; they do not replace it.
whyNot.1: Reporting supports control but cannot guarantee the outcome.
whyNot.2: Decision gates are a governance control in their own right; reports inform them.

B.q: A key supplier goes into administration and the project manager reports this to the sponsor straight away. What type of reporting is this?
B.why: A report triggered by a significant event, rather than the calendar, is event-driven.

whyNot.1: Time-driven reports follow a regular cycle, not a sudden event.
whyNot.2: 'Benefits-driven' is not a recognised type of progress report.
whyNot.3: 'Schedule-driven' is not a recognised type of progress report.

B.q: A project manager reports at every decision gate and whenever a tolerance is threatened, but never on a regular cycle. Which type of reporting is missing?
B.why: Gate and tolerance reports are event-driven. What is missing is regular, time-driven reporting that gives a steady picture and shows trends.

whyNot.1: Reports at gates and on threatened tolerances are already event-driven.
whyNot.2: Reporting when a tolerance is threatened is exception reporting, which is already happening.
whyNot.3: Gate reports are milestone-type reports, which are already happening.

C.q:
Which THREE of the following are benefits of progress reporting?
1) Better-informed decision-making
2) Forecasting when the project will finish
3) An audit trail of performance over time
4) Removing all risk from the project
C.why: Informed decisions (1), forecasting (2) and an audit trail (3) are all benefits of progress reporting.

whyNot.0: Statement 4 is wrong: no process can remove all risk from a project.
whyNot.1: Statement 4 is wrong: reporting highlights risks but cannot remove them.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong, and statement 1 is a key benefit that has been left out.

C.q: A sponsor notes that every monthly report showed Green, yet the project has suddenly announced a three-month delay. What has most likely failed?
options: The reports did not reflect the true status
The decision gates were held too frequently
The estimating funnel was drawn too narrowly
The product owner reprioritised the backlog
C.why: If reports stayed Green while a major delay built up, they were not reflecting actual performance against the baseline, so the early warning was lost.

whyNot.1: Frequent gates would give more chances to spot problems, not fewer.
whyNot.2: The funnel concerns estimating accuracy; it does not explain misleading status reports.
whyNot.3: Reprioritising a backlog adjusts scope; it does not explain reports hiding a delay.

C.q: A board receives clear progress reports, sees costs trending above baseline, and agrees recovery actions in time. Which benefit of reporting does this illustrate?
C.why: Reporting variance early allowed the board to make timely decisions and take corrective action.

whyNot.0: Motivation may follow, but the scenario shows decision-making and correction.
whyNot.1: Nothing in the scenario relates to procurement costs.
whyNot.3: Good reporting builds stakeholder engagement; it does not aim to lower interest.

reteach.title: Building a music festival site
reteach.question: A festival director is three hours away while the site is built. How does she know whether the gates will open on time?

blocks.h: Updates on a rhythm, and calls when it matters
blocks.body: Every evening the site manager sends a short update: stages built, fencing done, toilets delivered, against the build plan. That is TIME-DRIVEN. When the main stage lorry breaks down, she phones the director at once: that is EVENT-DRIVEN. Each area on the update has a colour: Green on track, Amber slipping but recoverable, Red needs the director's decision.

blocks.text: The director can only rescue the main stage because she hears about it in time. Early, honest reporting is what makes decisions possible.

explain.body: Progress reporting communicates status, actual performance against the baseline, to the sponsor and stakeholders, so they can make timely decisions and take corrective action.

test.q: Who is the main audience for a project progress report?
test.why: Progress reports are mainly for the sponsor and stakeholders who need status information to make decisions.

whyNot.0: The team may see reports too, but the main purpose is to inform the sponsor and stakeholders.
whyNot.2: Competitors are not an audience for internal project reports.
whyNot.3: Auditors may use reports as an audit trail, but they are not the main audience.

explain.body: Early warning of variances, informed decision-making, forecasting of completion, transparency and accountability, stakeholder confidence, an audit trail, and visibility of risks and issues.

explain.caption: Also: transparency, stakeholder confidence, an audit trail, and visibility of risks and issues.

test.q: Which of these is NOT a benefit of progress reporting?
test.why: Reporting does not change the schedule's logic, so it cannot shorten the critical path.

whyNot.0: Transparency and accountability are benefits of reporting.
whyNot.1: Honest, regular reports build stakeholder confidence.
whyNot.2: Reports create a record of performance and decisions over time.

explain.body: Time-driven reports follow a regular cycle, such as weekly or monthly. Event-driven reports are triggered by something happening: a milestone, a decision gate or an exception when a tolerance is threatened.

test.q:
Which TWO events would typically trigger an event-driven report?
1) Reaching a key milestone
2) The first Monday of each month
3) A tolerance about to be breached
4) The end of each financial quarter
test.why: Reaching a milestone (1) and a threatened tolerance (3) are events, so they trigger event-driven reports.

whyNot.0: The first Monday of each month (2) is a calendar trigger, so it is time-driven.
whyNot.1: Both 2 and 4 are calendar triggers, so these are time-driven reports.
whyNot.3: The end of a quarter (4) is a calendar trigger, so it is time-driven.

explain.body: RAG gives an at-a-glance view. Green: on track against the baseline. Amber: problems that should be recoverable within tolerance. Red: off track, with tolerance breached or about to be, needing a decision.

test.q: A workstream is reported as Red. What does this usually mean?
options: It is on track and within plan
It is off track and needs intervention
It has minor issues being managed
It has been completed and closed
test.why: Red usually means the work is off track, with tolerance breached or about to be, and needs a decision or intervention.

whyNot.0: On track and within plan is Green.
whyNot.2: Minor, recoverable issues are usually Amber.
whyNot.3: RAG shows status against the baseline, not whether work is closed.
